paper_title: ReFocus: Progress-Guided Adaptive Practice for Long-Horizon Robotic Manipulation Reinforcement Learning

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Online reinforcement learning (RL) enables vision-language-action policies to improve through environmental interaction. However, in long-horizon manipulation, sparse success/failure feedback provides little information about where policies encounter bottlenecks. Moreover, repeated full-task rollouts also leave these bottlenecks weakly analyzed and insufficiently practiced. To this end, we introduce ReFocus, a progress-guided multi-round RL framework that alternates between Global and Local RL to identify task-specific bottlenecks and allocate additional practice to them. Specifically, during Global RL, we decompose each task into a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) of subtasks. Then a DAG-based Progress Reward is leveraged for both policy training and bottleneck diagnosis. Based on the identified bottlenecks, ReFocus selects Adaptive Practice Windows, defining task segments from an entry stage to a target stage. It allocates additional interaction to these segments during Local RL while updating the entire policy. After that, it evaluates the policy to perform the full task for the next round of RL, forming an iteration between Global and Local RL. Experiments on LIBERO-Long and RoboCasa365 show that ReFocus achieves success rates of 97.8% and 51.3%, respectively, compared with 90.6% and 39.3% for the $π_{0.5}$ baseline. Furthermore, we evaluate a real-world adaptation on three long-horizon tasks. On BreadBaker, ReFocus achieves 95% success, compared with 30% for the $π_{0.5}$. Project page: https:// refocus-robotics.github.io/ 1. Introduction In long-horizon manipulation, the success of subtask depends on both its execution and the state inherited from preceding stages. Completing one subtask therefore does not guarantee successful continuation. Imitation learning gives vision-language-action (VLA) policies strong initialization by supervising actions along expert trajectoCorresponding authors. 1 ries [5, 6, 34]. At deployment, however, successive subtasks begin from states produced by the policy itself, and demonstrations provide limited supervision for handling the deviations that accumulate along the way, resulting in failure. Online reinforcement learning (RL) enables VLA policies to learn beyond demonstrations with further environmental interactions by themselves. However, most online RL methods, which learn from full-task rollouts using only binary terminal feedback, still struggle with long-horizon tasks. As illustrated in Fig. 1(a), two episodes with different failuresone from bowl transport and the other from shelf placementreceive the same zero reward despite different amounts of completed work. Our diagnostic further reveals concentrations of failures at specific stages, as shown in Figs. 8 and 9 of Appendix A. Although some work recovers intermediate supervision by estimating progress between observations or rewarding verifiable subtask completions [41, 51], two challenges remain: 1) Reward Imbalance. To characterize intermediate progress, we group verifiable subtasks with shared prerequisites into stages, within which subtasks can be completed in any order. Even with prerequisite gating and one-time credit, the total reward assigned to stage can depend on its decomposition granularity. Uniform per-subtask rewards, for example, give stage more weight simply because it contains more completion events. 2) Limited Bottleneck Practice. Under fixed interaction budget, the stage limiting full-task success can receive few opportunities for practice and less comprehensive analysis. For example, in Fig. 1(a), each new attempt at shelf placement requires another grasp and transport, and an earlier failure prevents that attempt altogether. Moreover, there is no deeper analysis of the reason for the failure of shelf placement. To this end, we introduce ReFocus, progress-guided RL framework for long-horizon manipulation. ReFocus alternates Global RL with Local RL to improve shared VLA policy. During Global RL, we represent each task as directed acyclic graph (DAG) of subtasks and their dependencies. To address Reward Imbalance, DAG-based Progress Reward allocates fixed task-level reward budget equally Figure 1. Motivation and overview of ReFocus. (a) Sparse terminal rewards reveal little about partial progress or task-specific bottlenecks. (b) ReFocus uses progress feedback to guide targeted practice through alternation of Global RL and Local RL. (c) ReFocus achieves success rates of 98.3% on three real-world long-horizon tasks, compared with 81.7% for RECAP [1]. (d) ReFocus raises the success rates of π0.5 [5] from 90.6% to 97.8% on LIBERO-Long and from 39.3% to 51.3% on RoboCasa365. across stages. Each stages share is then divided equally among its subtasks. The total budget allocated to stage is therefore independent of its number of subtasks, preventing finer decompositions from receiving disproportionate weight. Subtask-completion records also provide structured evidence of task progress to support bottleneck diagnosis. Based on progress feedback, an LLM-based Scheduler identifies stages where the policy repeatedly stalls and selects Adaptive Practice Windows for Local RL. Normal window rollouts concentrate practice on the selected bottleneck, while prefix window and suffix window rollouts connect it with execution from the normal task start and continuation toward full-task completion, respectively. Milestone rewards provide finer feedback within the selected task segment. Together, these rollout modes connect targeted practice with the states inherited from earlier stages and the requirements of later stages. After each round, evaluations assess task progress and full-task success. The Scheduler uses these results, previous windows, and interaction costs to retain, revise, or skip subsequent practice windows. By keeping practice allocation aligned with the remaining difficulties, multi-round training helps translate local gains into progressively more reliable full-task execution. We evaluate ReFocus on LIBERO-Long [27] and RoboCasa365 [33]. Based on supervised finetuning (SFT) baseline π0.5 [5], ReFocus improves its performance from 90.6% and 39.3% to 97.8% and 51.3% respectively. On three long-horizon real-world tasks, we compare RECAPbased adaptation of ReFocus with SFT and RECAP [1]. On BreadBaker, RECAP improves the success rate from 30% to 70%. ReFocus further increases it to 95%. ReFocus also achieves 100% on both StackBowl and PickFruit, compared with 90% and 85% for RECAP, respectively. We introduce ReFocus, progress-guided RL framework that alternates Global RL with Local RL to identify taskspecific bottlenecks and allocate targeted practice in longhorizon manipulation. ReFocus uses DAG-based progress rewards during Global RL to provide dense feedback and identify bottleneck subtasks. Adaptive Practice Windows then focus Local RL on these bottlenecks. Extensive experiments show that ReFocus improves the long-horizon manipulation performance of SFT baselines on the LIBERO-Long and RoboCasa365 benchmarks and on real-world manipulation tasks. 2. Related Work Robotic Foundation Models. Large-scale robot demonstrations enable VLA models to learn generalist manipulation across diverse tasks and embodiments [5, 6, 23, 34]. Recent efforts further scale heterogeneous robot data to improve policy capabilities [32, 46, 47, 52, 54]. Embodied reasoning and steerable conditioning support multi-step execution [19, 37], while world-action models integrate visual 2 Figure 2. Illustration of ReFocus. (a) Global RL uses task DAGs to assign progress rewards and track subtask completion. (b) The Scheduler selects Adaptive Practice Windows for bottleneck practice. Three rollout modes connect local practice with full-task execution, while milestone rewards provide finer feedback. (c) Multi-round training alternates Global and Local RL. Full-task feedback and practice costs are recorded in the history buffer to guide subsequent practice. prediction with robot control [21, 35, 50]. However, policies trained on demonstrations may struggle with unfamiliar states and accumulated errors during long-horizon manipulation, motivating further improvement through RL. Reinforcement Learning for VLAs. Reinforcement learning improves pretrained VLA policies using offline data or online interaction. Offline methods use preferences, action values, or recovery data [18, 20, 56], while online methods optimize policies with actorcritic or group-relative objectives [11, 25, 29, 31]. Further work studies efficient training and real-world adaptation [1, 9, 13, 43, 45, 53]. For longhorizon tasks, terminal outcomes provide limited feedback on partially completed trajectories. To provide feedback beyond task outcomes, reward and critic models incorporate intermediate progress [15, 24, 26, 41, 55], stage structure [8, 16], or execution history [12, 49]. Building on these approaches, ReFocus uses DAG-based progress feedback to allocate equal reward budgets across stages and credit subtask completions according to prerequisites. Long-Horizon Manipulation. Long-horizon tasks require policies to complete multiple subtasks while handling errors accumulated during execution. Prior work addresses long-horizon tasks by incorporating subtask prerequisites or downstream success into rewards [30, 51]. Other approaches focus learning on difficult subtasks through specialist policies [22, 28, 40], or allocate practice using budget-aware scheduling, reset curricula, and task selection [4, 14, 17, 42]. Execution feedback has also been used to improve skills and policies across iterations [10, 44, 48]. In contrast, ReFocus adaptively selects task-specific practice windows across rounds using subtask progress, fulltask evaluations, and practice history. 3. Method In this section, we first introduce Global RL with Progress Reward for full-task policy learning (3.1). We then present Local RL, which directs interaction toward stages requiring further improvement (3.2). Finally, we describe the optimization paradigm that alternates between phases to improve shared policy across training rounds (3.3). The overall pipeline of ReFocus is shown in Fig. 2. 3.1. Global RL with Progress Reward We consider set of long-horizon manipulation tasks and shared VLA policy πθ initialized through supervised finetuning (SFT). Global RL optimizes this policy using full-task rollouts. Experiments 4.1. Experimental Setup Benchmarks and Evaluation Settings. We conduct experiments on RoboCasa365 Composite-seen [33] and LIBERO-Long [27]. Compared with tasks centered on individual skills, these benchmarks require sustained progress across multiple subgoals, making them suitable for studying intermediate feedback and targeted practice. LIBEROLong contains 10 tabletop tasks involving multiple objects and goal conditions. We also use 16 Composite-Seen tasks from RoboCasa365 that extend evaluation to diverse kitchen activities involving object transport and appliance interaction. For each benchmark, we initialize π0.5 through SFT on the official demonstrations and subsequently train shared policy across all selected tasks. Validation rollouts are used to diagnose bottlenecks and guide practice-window selection. We evaluate each policy on 50 and 100 initial scenarios per task for LIBERO-Long and RoboCasa365. Baselines. We compare ReFocus with the SFT-initialized π0.5 policy and four representative methods: SparseRL [53], SimpleVLA-RL [25], PolicyTrim [45], and StructRL [51]. Sparse-RL PPO uses binary success reward for PPO, while StructRL provides subtask-level progressreward baseline. All RL baselines use the same training configuration. More details about training and evaluation configurations are provided in Appendix C. 4.2. Main Results Overall Performance. Table 1 compares ReFocus with SFT and representative RL post-training methods. ReFocus achieves the highest overall success rates on both benchmarks, reaching 51.3% on RoboCasa365 and 97.8% on LIBERO-Long, exceeding the SFT baseline by 12.0 and 7.2 points, respectively. Compared with Sparse-reward PPO [53], it improves by 10.2 and 5.2 points. ReFocus also outperforms StructRL [51] by 5.5 and 1.6 points, respectively. The gains over both sparseand structured-reward baselines support the effectiveness of combining progress feedback with adaptive practice. Performance across Task Horizons. Ablation Study The main benchmark results demonstrate the effectiveness of ReFocus. We further examine Progress Reward, Practice Window, Local RL rollout mixtures, and the allocation of progress feedback. We also examine credit assignment and performance gains across optimization rounds. Component Ablation. Table 2 examines Progress Reward and Practice Window on LIBERO-Long. When Progress Reward is disabled, subtask checks and progress records remain available for diagnosis and window selection. From the Sparse-RL PPO baseline of 92.6%, adding Progress Reward or Practice Window alone increases success to 96.8% and 93.4%, respectively. Combining both reaches 97.8%. Modes are sampled at rollout resets, with normal-start full-task rollouts as fallback for tasks without an eligible window. Normal window-only practice achieves 95.4% success, increasing to 96.4% with suffix window, 96.8% with prefix window, and 97.8% with both. On the longest tasks, Suffix improves success from 88.0% to 92.0%, compared with 90.0% for Prefix. Conclusion In this work, we present ReFocus, progress-guided multiround RL framework for long-horizon manipulation that alternates Global and Local RL to improve shared VLA policy. Specifically, during Global RL, DAG-based Progress Reward balances reward allocation across stages for policy training and supports bottleneck diagnosis. After identifying bottlenecks, Adaptive Practice Windows concentrate additional interaction on the corresponding bottlenecks during Local RL. Experiments on LIBERO-Long and RoboFigure 7. Real-world task setups. We conduct three long-horizon tasks, with circled numbers indicating the order of execution. 4.4. Real-World Experiments Experimental Setup. We deploy the policies on Unitree G1-D humanoid robot. The policy takes RGB images from the right head-mounted camera and both wrist cameras, and outputs joint positions for both arms and gripper actions. We conduct experiments on three tasks, as shown in Fig. 7. For each task, we collect 50 human demonstrations to initialize the π0.5 policy, followed by 50 autonomous rollouts. Baselines. We compare SFT, RECAP [1], and ReFocusbased adaptation. Since online PPO rollouts and intermediate-state resets are costly on physical robots, we adopt RECAP for post-training. GPT-6 Astra [36] serves as the Scheduler, identifying subtask progress and bottlenecks from rollout observations. We incorporate Progress Rewards when training the value function and computing advantages. We also upsample bottleneck segments alongside full-task rollouts. Each policy is evaluated over three runs of 20 trials per task. Quantitative Results. Table 5 reports average success rates per task. ReFocus achieves 100%, 100%, and 95% success on StackBowl, PickFruit, and BreadBaker, respectively. The largest gain occurs on BreadBaker, which requires coordinating bread grasping, transport, insertion, 8 Casa365 show that ReFocus improves the SFT baseline from 90.6% and 39.3% to 97.8% and 51.3%, respectively. RECAP-based adaptation extends the framework to three real-world tasks, achieving 95% success on BREADBAKER compared with 30% for the SFT-initialized π0.5 policy.

sections.content: 14 14 14 15 17 21 22 22 23 23 23 23 25 25 26 27 27 13 A. Failure-Stage Analysis Fig. 8 summarizes task-specific failure patterns during Global RL. We collect five normal-start validation rollouts per task at each of five checkpoints across the 16 RoboCasa365 Composite-Seen tasks, yielding 400 rollouts and 228 failures. Numbers inside the bars indicate failure counts, and the right-hand labels show failed/total rollouts per task. Figure 9 highlights three In GetToastedBread, 17 of 19 failures occur at the initial toastertasks with failures concentrated at different stages. activation stage. In KettleBoiling, 9 of 11 failures occur at burner activation after the kettle has been placed on the stove. In StirVegetables, 10 of 15 failures occur at the final stirring stage. These results reveal distinct bottlenecks at early, intermediate, and late stages across tasks. Despite these differences in completed subtasks and remaining difficulties, all failed rollouts receive the same terminal failure feedback. This feedback alone provides little guidance on which actions made valid progress or which stages require further practice. These observations motivate using subtask-level progress to identify task-specific bottlenecks and direct additional practice toward the stages that remain difficult. Figure 8. Failure-stage distributions on RoboCasa365. Bars show the first unfinished stage in archived validation rollouts. Figure 9. Task-specific bottlenecks in three representative tasks. Stage descriptions and counts are provided alongside. B. Method Details In this section, we provide more details about the task specifications and completion checks (B.1), the state-storage and restoration procedure (B.2), and the Scheduler inputs and complete prompt templates (B.3). B.1. Task Specifications and Completion Checks We implement the completion conditions proposed by the Scheduler using task-specific simulator checks, including object receptacle relations, fixture states, and cumulative activity checks. Tables 6 and 7 list the stage definitions for RoboCasa365 and LIBERO-Long, respectively. At each reward evaluation, completion checks use the preceding progress state to determine eligibility. Newly valid events are collected before advancing the active stage, so future-stage predicates are not credited in the same evaluation. Each event is recorded once and contributes to the reward of its action chunk. Table 8 illustrates milestone refinements within the target subtasks of six recorded practice windows. The examples use available simulator signals to provide finer feedback for object transport, fixture operation, insertion, and continuous activity. Table 9 gives three corresponding examples for LIBERO-Long, with target subtasks taken directly from Table 7. 14 Table 6. Refined Task DAGs for RoboCasa365 Composite-Seen. Since comparable mid-episode resets are impractical on physical hardware, the real-world experiments of ReFocus employ RECAP-based post-training on recorded rollouts as an alternative. In current version, ReFocus employs frontier LLM as the Scheduler, which operates between training rounds to diagnose execution bottlenecks and allocate practice windows accordingly. direction for future work is to extend from an inter-round advisor to an online Co-Worker that remains active throughout task execution. Under this paradigm, when the VLA policy stalls at bottleneck subtask, the Co-Worker would intervene by selecting and triggering an appropriate recovery skill, temporarily assuming control until task progress is verified, at which point execution would be returned to the policy.
